Wednesday
Spent the whole free period explaining moles to Deepika and I'm exhausted. I told her: a mole is just Avogadro's number of particles, so you divide the given mass by the molar mass and boom, you have moles. Then multiply by N-A for particles. Literally two steps. She kept saying "wait, what's molar mass?" and "why that number?" I said it three times, faster each time, and she just went quiet and copied my notes.
I don't get it. It's SO simple. Maybe she's just not a science person.
Though now that I think of it, I only understood it after Sir did that thing with the bag of rice grains for a whole class. I'd forgotten that.
- Trisha

qa.q: What did Deepika keep asking?
qa.a: "Wait, what's molar mass?" and "why that number?"

qa.q: Why does Trisha decide Deepika is "just not a science person"?
qa.a: To Trisha, moles feel like 'literally two steps', so it's hard to see why anyone would struggle, and blaming the listener feels more natural than doubting the explanation.

qa.q: What could Trisha try in the next free period?
qa.a: Start from what Deepika already knows, explain molar mass in plain words, go slowly, and maybe use something like the rice-grain bag that once helped Trisha.

qa.q: What might the free period have felt like for Deepika?
qa.a: Deepika may have felt more lost and embarrassed each time it was repeated faster, so she went quiet and just copied the notes.

grounding: It shows a teenager explaining a topic too fast with jargon and then judging the listener as slow.

After school in Kinhai village, Pallavi stayed back to help Uday with the Class 9 science practical. She had topped the district quiz, and acids and bases felt like her own language.
"Simple," she said, dipping the paper strip. "pH below seven is acidic, so more H-plus ions; above seven, more OH-minus. Neutralisation gives salt and water. Done."
Uday stared at the strip. "Ions?"
"H-plus. Hydrogen ions. I just said."
"And why does the colour change?"
"Indicator!" Pallavi tapped the bottle, a little sharply. The bell for the last bus rang. "Honestly, Uday, it's the easiest chapter."
Uday packed his bag without a word. On the bus, Pallavi watched the fields go by and wondered why he never seemed to get anything.

qa.q: What had Pallavi topped?
qa.a: The district quiz.

qa.q: Why does Pallavi wonder why Uday never seems to get anything?
qa.a: Acids and bases feel like her own language, so she can't see that words like 'ions' and 'indicator' are new to him, and she reads his confusion as slowness.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do differently at the next practical?
qa.a: Start with something Uday knows, like lemon juice being sour, explain one word at a time, and let him say back what the colour change means.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling as he packed his bag without a word?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and a little hurt after being told it's the easiest chapter, and unwilling to ask more.

grounding: It shows a teenager who knows a topic well rushing through it with jargon and then thinking the classmate is slow.

The seminar hall at the engineering college held sixty first-years, and Naveen, a final-year, had been invited to talk about his summer internship. He clicked to his first slide. "So basically we built an ETL pipeline feeding an LLM with RAG, deployed on K8s, with CI/CD for the MLOps side."
In the third row, Suraj stopped writing. Around Suraj, pens paused. Someone opened a phone under the desk.
Naveen kept going, faster, pleased with how smoothly it was flowing. "Obviously the latency on the vector DB was the bottleneck."
By minute four, half the hall was looking at the ceiling fans.
At the end there were no questions. Naveen walked out a little annoyed. "Tough crowd," he told the coordinator. "I kept it really basic."

qa.q: How many first-years were in the seminar hall?
qa.a: Sixty first-years.

qa.q: Why did Naveen feel he had kept it really basic?
qa.a: Naveen felt pleased with how smoothly it flowed because those terms were everyday words in his internship, so they seemed basic to him and he couldn't see that first-years had never heard them.

qa.q: What could Naveen have done in his first minute instead?
qa.a: Say in plain words what the project did, with one everyday example, and explain any acronym he truly needed before using it.

qa.q: What was the talk like for Suraj in the third row?
qa.a: Suraj stopped writing almost immediately, likely feeling lost and maybe a bit resentful at being made to feel behind.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming first-years know his acronyms and losing them within the first minute.

Today's outreach talk at the girls' school was a disaster, and honestly I don't know what more I could have done. I spent two weeks on the slides! Elizabeth

passage: I'm Disha, I inspect old bridges for the city, and last year I had to explain to a residents' meeting why their footbridge had to close. My report was full of words like "fatigue cracking" and "load rating". So the night before, I tried it on my younger brother Anand, who sells phones and has zero interest in engineering. First attempt, he yawned. So I switched. "Bend a steel spoon back and forth. It doesn't break the first time, but it will. That's what the trucks rumbling underneath do to this bridge's joints." Then I asked him to tell it back to me. He said, "Didi, it's getting tired, like a spoon." Perfect. At the meeting I used the spoon, and an aunty in the front row said, "Close it, then."

qa.q: What everyday object did Disha use to explain the bridge?
qa.a: A steel spoon bent back and forth.

qa.q: Why did Disha try the explanation on Anand the night before?
qa.a: Disha was worried the residents would not follow a report full of technical words, so she tested it on Anand, someone outside engineering, to see whether ordinary people could understand it.

qa.q: Which step in Disha's method worked best, and why?
qa.a: Asking Anand to tell it back, because his answer, 'it's getting tired, like a spoon', proved the idea had landed in plain words. 👍

qa.q: How might the residents have felt if Disha had just read out 'fatigue cracking' and 'load rating'?
qa.a: They might have felt confused or suspicious that the bridge was closing for no clear reason, instead of agreeing to close it.

grounding: It shows a skilled engineer testing her explanation on someone outside the field, using a plain example, and asking him to say it back.

passage: I'm Sachin, and I've worked with Kashish for two years, so I've watched her explain our billing software to plenty of clients. qa.q: What made Kashish's explanation on the call work?
qa.a: A plain comparison with ticking off a bill book, a real bill from his own shop, and asking him to say in his own words what it would do.

qa.q: What might the call have been like for Mr. Kutty?
qa.a: He likely felt respected rather than lost, since the explanation used his own bill and let him put it in his own words.

Yash (Class 10) came in today on his own. After Friday's annual day, where he danced a solo, a senior in the corridor laughed and said he "moved like a broken robot". Yash has replayed that line, by his own count, "about a hundred times". qa.a: Seeing every comment laid out, one unkind next to many kind ones, lets him weigh them fairly instead of replaying one line.

qa.a: Aadhya might feel a little hurt that a sincere card didn't reach Yash, and want him to know it was meant.

qa.a: Elizabeth might be worried about Salma's mood and want to gently point out that the metro ride went fine.

passage: For the campus radio's Honest Hour, this is Lakshmi. Last semester I got hooked on bad news. It started with one cyclone update. Then I'd wake at 3 a.m. and check: more storms, a bridge collapse, a post saying our generation has no future, a thread about layoffs. Every refresh felt like keeping watch, as if something would sneak up on me if I stopped. My roommate Sangeeta would ask, "Anything new?" and honestly, most nights, no. Same stories, new angry comments. But my heart would be racing and I'd skip breakfast. I told Sangeeta the world was ending. She asked what I'd do differently if it was. I had no answer. I just knew I felt terrible, and scrolling didn't make me know any more.

qa.q: At what time would Lakshmi wake up and check the news?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: Why did scrolling feel like "keeping watch" to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt anxious that stopping would let something bad sneak up, so each refresh felt like protection and the checking felt necessary even though it brought no new information.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi have done on those 3 a.m. nights?
qa.a: Keep the phone out of reach at night, and if the worry stays heavy, talk to Sangeeta or the college counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Sangeeta to share a room with Lakshmi then?
qa.a: Sangeeta likely saw the racing heart and skipped breakfasts and felt worried, asking gentle questions to help Lakshmi notice nothing new was being learned.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news at night, feeling the world is ending while gaining no real information.

passage:
The one-star review arrived at nine: "Blouse fitting was off. Won't come back." Sarita, twenty-five, read it twice in her little tailoring shop in Jaipur and felt her stomach drop.
Himani, cutting fabric at the next table, winced. "Ouch."
Sarita took out the green notebook she kept in the drawer. "Before I decide this week was bad, let's count." She wrote: twelve orders delivered on time. Mrs. Rathore's thank-you note. The bride who sent a photo. Two customers who came back with friends. Then, in a separate column: one fitting complaint.
"So one miss out of fifteen," Himani said.
"A real miss. I'll call her and offer to fix it," Sarita said. "But it's one line, not the whole book."

qa.q: What did the one-star review say?
qa.a: "Blouse fitting was off. Won't come back."

qa.q: Why does Sarita reach for the green notebook right after the review?
qa.a: Sarita feels hurt by the review and knows one sharp review can feel like the whole week, so she wants to see the good things next to the bad before deciding how things are going.

qa.q: How does Sarita take the complaint seriously without overreacting?
qa.a: She calls it a real miss and plans to offer a fix, but writes it as one line beside twelve on-time orders and happy customers.

qa.q: How might the unhappy customer feel if Sarita calls to fix the blouse?
qa.a: The customer might feel heard and surprised, and perhaps less sure about never coming back. 🙂

grounding: It shows a grounded young woman counting her wins alongside a setback before judging how her week went.

passage:
"So? How was the appraisal?" Vijay asked, handing his wife a plate of poha.
"My manager said my reports are late sometimes," Preeti said.
"Oh no."
"Wait, I'm not done." She pulled out a folded paper. "I wrote down everything she said, good and bad, before I could forget the good parts. She said my client calls are the best on the team. She said the new joinees come to me for help. She said the Pune project went well because of me. And reports are late sometimes."
"That's three good, one bad."
"Exactly. On the bus I could feel the late-reports thing getting louder, so I read the list twice."
"And the reports?"
"Real. I'll block Friday mornings for them." She took a spoonful. "But I'm not calling it a bad appraisal."

qa.q: What did Preeti's manager say about the new joinees?
qa.a: That they come to her for help.

qa.q: Why did Preeti write down everything the manager said so quickly?
qa.a: She expected the criticism to get louder in her head and the praise to fade, so she wanted a fair record of both.

qa.q: How does Preeti respond to the one piece of criticism?
qa.a: She accepts it as real and plans to block Friday mornings for reports, without letting it turn the whole appraisal bad.

qa.q: How might Vijay's evening have gone if Preeti had come home talking only about late reports?
qa.a: Vijay might have spent the evening consoling her about a 'bad' appraisal that was actually mostly good.

grounding: It shows a grounded young woman giving praise the same weight as criticism before deciding how her appraisal went.

passage: Last March, after my under-14 team lost 4-0 in the district semi-final, I sat in the bus and decided I was a terrible coach. I'm Varun, I'd coached them for one season, and all I could see were the four goals. That night Nitin, my assistant, made me do something I now do after every tournament. We wrote two lists. Losses: the semi-final, one group match. Wins: eight matches, two shy kids who now speak up in the huddle, zero injuries, the whole squad still turning up at 6 a.m. in winter. The second list was longer, and just as true. I still went over what went wrong in the semi, because that mattered. But I stayed. We're in the final this year.

qa.q: What was the score in the district semi-final?
qa.a: The team lost 4-0.

qa.q: Why did Varun feel like a terrible coach on the bus ride back?
qa.a: Varun felt crushed because the painful loss filled Varun's view, so the four goals felt like the whole season even though much had gone well.

qa.q: What is useful about the two-list habit?
qa.a: It puts the wins on the page beside the losses, so decisions rest on the whole record, while still leaving room to study what went wrong.

qa.q: What would have changed for the players if Varun had quit after the semi-final?
qa.a: The shy kids who now speak up and the squad who turned up in winter would have lost a coach who helped them, and might not have reached this year's final.

grounding: It shows a young coach listing wins alongside losses before deciding how the season went.

passage:
Papa was calling from the ship, and the network kept cutting out, so Kunal, nine, had only two minutes. "Tell me about your week, champ!"
Kunal gripped the phone. "Today Jaiswal sir made us stand outside for talking. He's the worst teacher."
His mother Hansa, sitting beside him, raised her eyebrows. On Monday Kunal had come home glowing because Jaiswal sir let him run the science experiment. On Wednesday he'd scored full marks in spelling. His big sister Arohi mouthed, "Tell him about the rocket!"
"Oh, and... um." Kunal frowned, trying to remember. The line crackled. "Standing outside was really bad, Papa."
The call dropped. Hansa smiled. "Next call, we'll make a list first."

qa.q: What happened at school today, according to Kunal?
qa.a: Jaiswal sir made them stand outside for talking.

qa.q: Why does Kunal call Jaiswal sir "the worst teacher"?
qa.a: Kunal feels upset about today's punishment, and because it is freshest in his mind it crowds out Monday's experiment, so the latest class seems like the whole truth about the teacher.

qa.q: How could Hansa's list idea help on the next call?
qa.a: Writing down something from each day before the call helps Kunal remember Monday and Wednesday, not only the last day.

qa.q: What might Papa think of Jaiswal sir after this call?
qa.a: Papa might think the teacher is harsh, without knowing Kunal loved running the science experiment earlier in the week.

grounding: It shows a boy, on a short phone call, describing his week only by the last day and judging a teacher by the latest class.

passage:
In their flat in Munirka, Delhi, Mawia's big sister Lalremsiami was filling in the school's weekly feedback form for him. "Which day of the week did you like best?"
"Friday," Mawia, eight, said at once. "We had the magic show."
"What about Tuesday? You went to the zoo! You talked about the tiger for hours."
Mawia scrunched his face. "Oh yeah. The tiger."
"And your teacher, Damini ma'am? Good or not good?"
"Not good. Yesterday she gave us extra homework."
"She also gave you a star for your poem on Wednesday."
"Did she?" Mawia genuinely couldn't remember.
Lalremsiami laughed and wrote "Friday" and "Tuesday" side by side.

qa.q: Where did Mawia go on Tuesday?
qa.a: The zoo.

qa.q: Why does Mawia rate Damini ma'am "not good"?
qa.a: Mawia still feels annoyed about the extra homework yesterday, the freshest thing he remembers about her, so it outweighs the star she gave him on Wednesday.

qa.q: How could the feedback form be filled in more fairly?
qa.a: Go through the week day by day with Mawia, as his sister started doing, before choosing a favourite day or judging the teacher.

qa.q: How might Damini ma'am feel reading "not good" because of one homework day?
qa.a: She might feel it's unfair, since earlier in the week she praised his poem with a star.

grounding: It shows a boy recalling mostly yesterday when asked about his week and judging his teacher by the last class.

"Faiz, how was your week?" his mother Farida asked, stirring the dal.
"Bad."
"Bad? All of it?"
"Deepika miss shouted at the whole class today because Nabeel threw chalk."
"And Monday?"
"Monday..." Faiz thought. "Monday was sports."
"Didn't you win the sack race on Monday?"
"Oh. Yes! I came first."
"And Wednesday?"
"Wednesday Deepika miss let me read my story to the class." He looked surprised. "She said it was the best one."
"So was it a bad week?"
Faiz dipped a finger in the dal and licked it. "Today was bad."
"Today was bad," Ammi agreed. "And the rest?"
"The rest was actually good."

qa.q: What did Faiz win on Monday?

qa.q: Why does Faiz first say his whole week was bad?
qa.a: Faiz feels upset about today's shouting, the most recent and loudest memory, so it colours the whole week until his mother reminds him of earlier days.

qa.q: How did Farida help Faiz see the week differently?
qa.a: She walked him back through Monday and Wednesday with questions, letting him remember the sack race and the story himself. 😊

qa.q: How might Deepika miss feel if she knew Faiz first called the week bad?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since on Wednesday she praised his story as the best one.

grounding: It shows a boy judging his whole week and his teacher by what happened today, until earlier days are recalled.

passage:
"I'm not going to Chaitanya's birthday," Pradeep announced, dropping his bag.
Amma looked up from the vegetables. "Since when?"
"Since today. He laughed when I missed the penalty. In front of everyone. He's a fake friend. Always has been."
"Always?"
"Always."
"The Chaitanya who sat with you every day when you broke your arm in Class 6?"
Pradeep paused. "That was ages ago."
"The one who shared his notes before the exams? Who came at midnight when Thatha was in hospital?"
"...He still laughed today."
"He did. That was mean, and you can tell him so. But is today the whole story of him?"
Pradeep kicked at the doormat. "It feels like it."

qa.q: When did Pradeep break his arm?
qa.a: In Class 6.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep call Chaitanya a fake friend who "always has been"?
qa.a: Today's laugh hurts and is the freshest memory, so it feels like the truth about Chaitanya and pushes years of kindness out of view.

qa.q: What does Amma suggest Pradeep can do about the laugh?
qa.a: Tell Chaitanya it was mean, rather than dropping the friendship, while remembering today isn't the whole story.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel if Pradeep skipped the birthday without a word?
qa.a: Chaitanya might be confused and hurt, perhaps without even realising how much the laugh stung.

grounding: It shows a teenager judging a long-time friend by the latest quarrel and forgetting years of kindness.

passage: Last month I almost blocked Sumit. We'd had a stupid fight over our chemistry project: he forgot the chart paper, I snapped, he snapped back, and he said I always act like the boss. That night all I could think was, "That's who Sumit really is. Careless and rude." I'm Mridul, and I've known Sumit since we were six. He taught me to ride a cycle. He stood up for me when some seniors mocked my stammer in Class 7. He once walked me home in the rain when I was sick. None of that came into my head that night, only the chart paper and "boss". My sister asked, "Is he really like that, or was he like that today?" It took me a week to answer.

qa.q: What did Sumit forget?
qa.a: The chart paper.

qa.q: Why did Mridul think that night that Sumit was "careless and rude"?
qa.a: Mridul felt angry after the fight, the most recent thing between them, so it seemed like the real Sumit, and years of kindness like the cycle and the stammer didn't come to mind.

qa.q: What does the sister's question help Mridul see?
qa.a: The difference between one bad day and who Sumit has been for years, so a single fight doesn't decide the whole friendship.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt during that week?
qa.a: Sumit might have been hurt by the fight too, and unsure whether a friendship going back to age six was over.

grounding: It shows a teenager treating the latest fight as the truth about a friend and forgetting years of kindness.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9B, Friday.
Shalini asked this morning to be moved away from Kavitha. They have sat together since Class 5. Yesterday they argued over a shared lunch box that was left open and ants got in; I heard raised voices. Shalini told me, "She's always been selfish, ma'am. I just didn't see it." When I asked for another example, she couldn't give one. Then she remembered, on her own, that Kavitha had brought her notes every day when she was ill for weeks last year, and she went quiet. I have not moved the seat yet. I suggested they each tell the other one thing they were upset about, with me nearby if they want. I'll check with both on Monday.

qa.q: How long have Shalini and Kavitha sat together?
qa.a: Since Class 5.

qa.q: Why does Shalini say Kavitha has "always been selfish"?
qa.a: Yesterday's argument is fresh and hurts, so it feels like the real Kavitha, even though Shalini can't name another example.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking for another example let Shalini remember Kavitha's kindness on her own, and not moving the seat yet gave the friendship a chance.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel if she learned Shalini wanted to change seats?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel shocked and hurt that one argument over a lunch box outweighed years of sitting together and bringing notes.

grounding: It shows a teenager judging a long-time friend by one recent quarrel and forgetting her past kindness.
